# Backups

Bay uses [restic](https://restic.net/) for deduplicated, encrypted backups to S3-compatible storage. Each accessory with backup enabled gets its own restic repository, systemd timer, and retention policy.

## How it works

1. **Per-accessory scripts** — the backup role generates a `backup-<name>.sh` script for each accessory
2. **Streaming**, restic runs each dump command and reads its output (`restic backup --stdin-from-command`), so there are no intermediate files on disk

   restic runs the dump command itself (`restic backup --stdin-from-command -- <dump command>`), for every method: `pg_dump`, `mysqldump`, the Redis `docker cp` and the `file` `docker cp`. When the dump command fails, also in the middle of the stream, restic stores no snapshot, so a cut-off dump never becomes the newest snapshot. The snapshot file names are the same as before (`<name>.sql`, `<name>-<db>.sql`, `<name>.rdb`, `<name>.tar`), so the restore commands do not change. The Redis restore did change: the `.rdb` snapshot is a tar archive that the restore now unpacks (see Restore below). This needs restic 0.17.0 or newer and older than 0.20.0 (tested up to 0.19.x), and the role stops when the box has another version. The role still installs 0.17.3 on a box with no restic and never upgrades a binary that is there.

   A failed dump sends `backup.failed` with `Dump command failed with exit code <n>, no snapshot stored (<file>)`. Bay reads the exit code from restic's error line (`command failed: exit status <n>`); the dump command's own error is in the journal. A dump command that exits 0 but writes nothing makes restic fail with `no data read`, and restic still stores a snapshot of the empty file. The script removes that snapshot (`restic forget <id>`, the id restic printed for this run), sends `backup.failed` with `Dump produced no data, no snapshot stored (<file>)` and exits 1. When restic fails for its own reason, the alert says `Restic backup failed with exit code <n> (<file>)`. With several databases, each one is its own snapshot: a failed database does not stop the next one, and the alert names the first failure.

   After the dumps, the script checks the size of every snapshot the run made. It reads the snapshot id from restic's `snapshot <id> saved` line and runs `restic stats <id> --json` for each one, so a run with several databases checks each database, not only the last. A snapshot under 100 bytes sends `backup.warning` with `Snapshot suspiciously small (<n> bytes, <file>)` and exits 1. The script reads the JSON from the last stdout line that starts with `{`, because restic 0.19 prints a progress line before the JSON of `stats --json` and restic 0.17 does not. Both versions work.
3. **Systemd timers** — replace cron with `Persistent=true` (catch up after downtime) and staggered scheduling
4. **Retention** — `restic forget --prune` runs after each backup to enforce retention policies
5. **Weekly maintenance** — `restic check` verifies repository integrity, `restic cache --cleanup` removes stale cache
6. **Deploy coordination** — backup scripts create lock files; deploys wait for active backups to finish before restarting containers

   The deploy waits for accessory backups and for volume backups (lock `<stack_name>_<volume>.lock`), up to 300 seconds each, then goes on.

## Enabling backups

Backups are **disabled by default**. To enable, add `backup_enabled: true` to your `group_vars/all/main.yml`:

```yaml
backup_enabled: true
```

Without this, the backup role is a no-op — no scripts, timers, or S3 connections are created.

## Prerequisites

- `backup_enabled: true` in `group_vars/all/main.yml`
- An S3-compatible storage bucket (AWS S3, Hetzner Object Storage, Backblaze B2, MinIO, etc.)
- API credentials with object-level permissions (`PutObject`, `GetObject`, `ListBucket`, `DeleteObject`)

You create the bucket manually — Bay only needs object-level permissions, not admin/CreateBucket access.

## Setup

### 1. Enable backups

Add `backup_enabled: true` to `group_vars/all/main.yml`.

### 2. Add credentials to vault

```bash
bay vault edit production
```

Add these variables inside the `secrets:` dict:

```yaml
secrets:
  # Shared S3 credentials (reused by backup role and other S3-aware services)
  S3_ENDPOINT: "s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com"
  S3_BUCKET: "my-bucket"
  S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID: "AKIA..."
  S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: "your-secret-key"

  # Restic encryption (generate with: bay secret)
  backup_restic_password: "a-strong-random-password"
```

The backup role reads `secrets.backup_s3_*` variables, which fall back to the shared `S3_*` vars automatically. You only need `secrets.backup_s3_*` overrides if backups should use different credentials or a different bucket than other services.

### 3. S3 endpoint reference

| Provider | Endpoint format | Example |
|----------|----------------|---------|
| **AWS S3** | `s3.<region>.amazonaws.com` | `s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com` |
| **Hetzner** | `<location>.your-objectstorage.com` | `fsn1.your-objectstorage.com` |
| **Backblaze B2** | `s3.<region>.backblazeb2.com` | `s3.us-west-004.backblazeb2.com` |
| **MinIO** | `<host>:<port>` | `minio.example.com:9000` |
| **DigitalOcean** | `<region>.digitaloceanspaces.com` | `fra1.digitaloceanspaces.com` |
| **Wasabi** | `s3.<region>.wasabisys.com` | `s3.eu-central-1.wasabisys.com` |

**AWS S3 tip:** Your endpoint is based on the bucket's region. Find it in the AWS Console under S3 > your bucket > Properties > "AWS Region". Then use `s3.<region>.amazonaws.com`. Common regions: `us-east-1`, `eu-central-1`, `eu-west-1`, `ap-southeast-1`.

### 4. Enable backup on an accessory

A fleet built from `bay.toml` files sets the backup in `bay.fleet.toml` on the shared resource,
and `method` is required there (see the [README](../README.md#backups)). `bay compile` writes
the `backup:` block into `services.yml`, always with its `method`. The image-name detection below
only applies to a hand-written `backup: true` in a `services.yml` that `bay compile` does not own.
In such a `services.yml`, add `backup: true` or an explicit config:

```yaml
accessories:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:17
    backup: true              # auto-detects pg_dump from image name
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    env:
      clear:
        POSTGRES_USER: app
        POSTGRES_DB: app
      secret:
        - POSTGRES_PASSWORD

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    backup: true              # auto-detects redis method

  # Explicit config (when image name doesn't match)
  vectordb:
    image: pgvector/pgvector:pg18
    backup:
      method: pg_dump         # required — image doesn't contain "postgres"
      schedule: "0 4 * * *"   # override: 4 AM daily (default: 3 AM)
      retain: 60              # override: keep 60 days (default: 30)
    volumes:
      - vectordb_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    env:
      clear:
        POSTGRES_USER: app
        POSTGRES_DB: vectors
```

### 5. Deploy

```bash
bay up production
```

Every `bay up` runs the backup role (since 2.23.2). It installs restic,
initializes the repo of each target, writes the backup scripts and enables the
systemd timers. `bay deploy production --tags backup` does the same without a
plan. A plain `bay deploy production` runs it when the box needs the rig.

Each deploy then checks every backup target of the box: the script must exist
and the timer `bay-backup@<target>.timer` must be enabled and active. A target
that is configured in `services.yml` but not installed fails the run, and the
error names it. This runs on `bay up`, a plain `bay deploy` and
`--tags deploy_stack` or `--tags backup`, and only reads (no restic, no S3). In
`--check` mode it only warns.

Before 2.23.2 `bay up` ran the backup role only when the plan had a `backup`
step. That step appeared once, when the config changed, and `bay up` commits
`services.yml` before it touches the box. So a first `bay up` that failed left
the target with no script and no timer, and no later plan had the step again.
A fleet resource with `backup` that got a new box never had a step at all.

## Auto-detection

When a hand-written `services.yml` has `backup: true`, the role detects the method from the image name. A `bay.fleet.toml` resource has no such detection: it must set `method`.

| Image contains | Method | Dump command |
|---------------|--------|-------------|
| `postgres` | `pg_dump` | `docker exec <name> pg_dump -U <user> <db>` |
| `mysql` or `mariadb` | `mysql` | `docker exec -e MYSQL_PWD=<password> <name> mysqldump -u <user> <db>` |
| `redis` | `redis` | `docker exec <name> redis-cli BGSAVE`, then `docker cp <name>:/data/dump.rdb -` |

`<name>` is the accessory key in `services.yml`. Bay creates the accessory container with
`docker run` under that name, so the script reaches it with `docker exec` and `docker cp`.
The rendered compose file only describes the stack. The script does not use `docker compose`.

If the image doesn't match any pattern and no explicit `method:` is set, the deploy **fails with an error** — it never silently falls back.

For `file` method (raw volume backup), you must set it explicitly with a `source_path`:

```yaml
backup:
  method: file
  source_path: /data
```

## Volume backups

A `bay.toml` volume mount with `backup` true, which is the default, is backed up too. `bay
compile` writes each one to `volume_backups:` in `services.yml` (see
[services.md](services.md#volume_backups)). The backup role then adds one `file` target per
volume whose container runs on the host:

- The target name is the Docker volume name, `<stack_name>_<volume>`, for example
  `bay_myapp-data`. The script is `backup-<target>.sh` and the repo ends in `/<target>/`.
- The script reads the mount path out of the container through the Docker daemon
  (`restic backup --stdin-from-command -- docker cp <container>:<path> -`). The unit runs as
  the app user, which cannot read the Docker data root itself.
- When `docker cp` fails, also in the middle of the copy, restic stores no snapshot. The
  script exits 1 and sends the `backup.failed` alert, and the newest snapshot stays the last
  good one.
- A deploy waits for a running volume backup before it recreates containers, like for an
  accessory backup: it waits for the lock `<stack_name>_<volume>.lock` up to 300 seconds.
- The project `[backup]` table, then `[defaults.backup]` in `bay.fleet.toml`, set the hour
  (UTC) and `keep` (whole days). Without either, `backup_schedule` and `backup_retain` apply.
- Nothing runs while `backup_enabled` is false. The plan says so: `volume backups are
  compiled, but backup_enabled is false: no backup runs`.
- A new or changed volume backup is a plan step of kind `backup`.
  `bay up` deploys the box of that volume (a one-project run deploys only the boxes it needs).
  It runs the `backup` tag on every run (since 2.23.2), so the script and the timer are
  installed in the same deploy, and a later `bay up` installs them when an earlier one failed.
- A volume that is gone, or set to `backup = false`, loses its timer and its script on the
  next deploy (since 2.24.0). The role removes only targets that its own manifest of the last
  run (`targets.json`) recorded, so a script it did not install is never touched. The restic
  repo stays: remove it by hand when you no longer need its snapshots.
- `backup = false` on the mount leaves the volume out. A volume from `bay import` carries it,
  because the old YAML fleet backed up no volume. Drop it to start the backups.

Restore a volume with `bay backup restore <env> <stack_name>_<volume>`. The restore stops
every running container that mounts the volume (found with `docker ps --filter volume=`, not
only the owner), reads the volume's mountpoint with `docker volume inspect`, extracts the
snapshot there as root (over the files that are there, it does not empty the volume first) and
starts the same containers again, also after a failure. A container that was stopped before
stays stopped. The pre-restore backup runs first, as for an accessory. Hosts that do not run
the container are skipped. When no targeted host runs the container, the restore fails and
names it, with nothing restored.

## Project databases (pg_dump)

A project backs up its own database with a `[services.<name>.backup]` table in `bay.toml`
(since 2.24.0). The service must be internal (no `path`, no `domain`), because only an internal
service compiles to an accessory, and the backup role backs up accessories.

```toml
[services.postgres]
image = "postgres:17"
memory = "2g"

[services.postgres.backup]
method = "pg_dump"          # required; the only method of this table
databases = ["app"]         # default: POSTGRES_DB of the service
hour = 2                    # UTC; default: the project [backup], then [defaults.backup]
keep = "30d"                # default: the same chain
format = "custom"           # custom (default, pg_dump -Fc) or plain (SQL text)
max_age_hours = 30          # the freshness check alerts after this many hours without a good run
```

`bay compile` writes it as the accessory's `backup:` block, with `utc: true` when an hour is set
and `clients`: the other containers of the project in that environment, which a live restore
stops first. A shared resource in `bay.fleet.toml` takes the same `databases`, `format` and
`max_age_hours` keys; its default `format` stays `plain`.

- **custom** runs `pg_dump -Fc -Z 0` and stores `<name>-<db>.dump`, also with one database.
  `-Z 0` leaves compression to restic, so unchanged tables give the same chunks every night
  and dedup. `pg_restore` can then restore with `--clean --if-exists`, without the production
  roles (`--no-owner`), or only some tables.
- **plain** stores SQL text, `<name>.sql` (`<name>-<db>.sql` with several databases), as before
  2.24.0.

Every pg_dump snapshot since 2.24.0 also carries the restic tag `db:<database>`. A restore goes
into the database the snapshot holds: its tag, else the `-<db>` of its file name. It never falls
back to `POSTGRES_DB`: with `databases = ["shop"]` and `POSTGRES_DB=main`, a restore of shop goes
into shop. A snapshot with neither (a one-database snapshot made before 2.24.0) holds an
unknown database: the config may have named another one when it was made. `latest` never
takes such a snapshot. Restore it with `--snapshot <id> --database <name>`; Bay then warns that
it cannot verify the content.

`max_age_hours` defaults to 1.25 times the longest gap between two runs of the schedule, and at
least `backup_max_age_hours` (30). A daily backup gets 30 hours, a weekly one 210.

A new, changed or removed database backup is a plan step of kind `backup` (`new database backup
of <name> (pg_dump)`). A change of only the `backup` table recreates no container: the backup key
is not in the container spec, so the plan shows no container `update`. `bay up` installs the
script and the timer in the same run.

Only a backup that restores is a backup. Prove it with `bay backup restore-test` (see Restore).

## Rig infrastructure: Headscale

The accessory loop above only covers things declared in `services.yml`. **Headscale**
— the tailnet coordination server — is rig infrastructure, not an accessory, so it was
historically never backed up. The backup role now captures its state automatically when
all of the following hold (no `services.yml` entry required):

- `backup_enabled: true`
- `access_gateway: headscale`
- the host is the control region (`headscale_server` is true / `region == headscale_control_region`)

What's backed up is the container's `/var/lib/headscale` (bind-mounted from
`/opt/headscale/data`): the sqlite node DB (`db.sqlite`) plus the noise and DERP private
keys (`noise_private.key`, `derp_server_private.key`). Losing these loses the tailnet
identity, every node's assigned IP, and the keys. The config dir (`/etc/headscale`,
`config.yaml` + `extra-records.json`) is re-rendered on every deploy and is intentionally
**not** backed up.

It is a `file`-method target with its own repo, systemd timer, retention, maintenance,
and Telegram alerting like every other target. Tune via `backup_headscale_*` (see Defaults),
or disable with `backup_headscale_state: false`.

The DB runs in SQLite WAL mode, so recent writes sit in `db.sqlite-wal` until a
checkpoint. A plain copy of the folder can catch `db.sqlite` and `db.sqlite-wal` at
different moments. So the backup does not copy the live files. The backup script
(`bay-backup@headscale`, runs as the app user) calls one root helper,
`/usr/local/sbin/bay-headscale-db-snapshot`, through a sudoers rule that allows it with
no arguments (`/etc/sudoers.d/bay-headscale-backup`). The helper:

1. runs `sqlite3 /opt/headscale/data/db.sqlite ".backup '<tmp>/headscale/db.sqlite'"`, the
   SQLite online backup API, while Headscale keeps running. `<tmp>` is a new 0700 folder in
   the root-only `/var/lib/bay-headscale-backup`, and the copy is 0600;
2. runs `PRAGMA integrity_check;` on the copy and stops with exit 1 unless it prints `ok`;
3. adds `noise_private.key` and `derp_server_private.key` (each when present);
4. writes a tar of these files to restic as `headscale.tar`, with the same `headscale/`
   folder as before, and removes the temp folder on every exit.

A failed step writes nothing to restic, so restic stores no snapshot and the script sends
the usual `backup.failed` alert ("Dump command failed with exit code 1"). The reason is in
the journal: `journalctl -u bay-backup@headscale`. The live `db.sqlite-wal` and
`db.sqlite-shm` are never in the archive. The backup role installs the distro `sqlite3`
package for the helper.

```bash
bay backup list headscale        # snapshots
bay backup run headscale         # back up now
bay backup status                # headscale appears alongside accessories
```

### Restoring Headscale (file-method restore)

`bay backup restore` is database-oriented (it streams into a container and runs
pg/redis validation), so restore the `file`-method headscale snapshot manually. On the
control host, as root, with the restic env loaded from `/opt/<stack>/backup/restic.env`:

```bash
set -a; . /opt/<stack>/backup/restic.env; set +a
export RESTIC_REPOSITORY="s3:$BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT/$BACKUP_S3_BUCKET/$BACKUP_S3_PREFIX/$(hostname)/headscale"

restic snapshots                                   # pick the snapshot to restore
docker stop headscale
# The archive holds db.sqlite alone. A -wal or -shm file left from the old DB would be
# replayed onto the restored one and corrupt it, so move them away first.
mkdir -p /root/headscale-pre-restore
mv /opt/headscale/data/db.sqlite* /root/headscale-pre-restore/
restic dump latest headscale.tar | tar -x -C /opt/headscale/data --strip-components=1
docker start headscale
bay gateway nodes                             # confirm nodes + IPs came back
```

The container is named `headscale` (`backup_headscale_container`). Bay creates it with
`docker run`, so stop and start it with `docker stop` and `docker start`. Do not use
`docker compose` here: the rendered compose file only describes the stack.

(`--strip-components=1` drops the leading `headscale/` directory of the archive so files
land directly under `/opt/headscale/data`. The files come back as root with mode 0600.
Snapshots made before the snapshot helper hold a raw `docker cp` of the folder, with the
`-wal` and `-shm` files of that moment; restore those the same way.)

### Restore test (Headscale)

Check a snapshot now and then without touching the live server. On the control host,
as root, with the restic env loaded as above:

```bash
SCRATCH=$(mktemp -d)                               # 0700, root only
restic dump latest headscale.tar | tar -x -C "$SCRATCH" --strip-components=1
ls -l "$SCRATCH"                                   # db.sqlite + the two keys, all 0600
sqlite3 "$SCRATCH/db.sqlite" 'PRAGMA integrity_check; select count(*) from nodes;'
rm -rf "$SCRATCH"
```

The first line of output must be `ok`, the second the node count that
`bay gateway nodes` shows (nodes that joined after the snapshot are missing). The folder
holds the private keys: remove it when you are done.

## Retention

The `retain` setting controls how long snapshots are kept:

**Simple form** (integer = days):
```yaml
backup_retain: 30           # global default
# or per-accessory:
backup:
  retain: 60                # keep 60 days
```
Maps to: `restic forget --keep-within 30d --prune`

**Structured form** (fine-grained):
```yaml
backup:
  retain:
    daily: 7
    weekly: 4
    monthly: 12
```
Maps to: `restic forget --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 --keep-monthly 12 --prune`

Retention runs after each successful backup. If pruning fails, the backup is still considered successful — pruning retries on the next run.

## CLI commands

`bay backup --help` is the command reference (list, run, restore, restore-test, status, check — each subcommand's `--help` carries examples).

## Restore

Restores stream data from restic directly into containers — no intermediate files (except Redis RDB which requires stop/copy/start).

The Redis snapshot `<name>.rdb` is a tar archive, not a bare RDB file: it holds what `docker cp <name>:/data/dump.rdb -` writes, one entry named `dump.rdb`. The restore stops the container, unpacks the archive with `docker cp - <name>:/data`, and starts the container again, also when the restore fails. Redis must be stopped while `dump.rdb` is replaced, because it saves its own data over the file when it shuts down. Before 2.4.0 the restore copied the archive as is to `/data/dump.rdb`, so Redis found a tar there.

Safety features:
- **Pre-restore backup** — automatically creates a snapshot tagged `pre-restore` before restoring
- **Confirmation required** — interactive prompt via CLI, or `-e confirm=yes` for direct ansible-playbook usage
- **Post-restore validation** — PostgreSQL checks table count > 0, Redis checks PONG response

A restore runs only on the host that backs up the target: each host has its own
restic repo, so a snapshot belongs to one host. When several hosts back up the
target (a shared resource on several boxes), `bay backup restore` stops and
lists them; name one with `--host <host>`. A name that no host backs up stops
the command before anything runs.

### PostgreSQL: scratch or live

`bay backup restore <env> <target>` on a pg_dump target restores into a **scratch** container
by default (since 2.24.0). It never touches the live database:

1. A new Postgres container of the same image starts with no network and no published port
   (`--network none`), so it trusts local connections and needs no secret. Its name starts with
   `bay-restore-test-`, and every command of the restore targets that name.
2. The snapshot is restored into it (`pg_restore --no-owner --no-privileges --exit-on-error`
   for custom, `psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 --single-transaction` for plain).
3. Every table is counted exactly and compared with the planner estimates of the live database
   (one read-only query). A table that is empty in the snapshot but not in the live estimates is
   named.
4. `bay backup restore` keeps the container for you to read
   (`docker exec -it <name> psql -U <user> <db>`). It is removed after `restore_keep_hours`
   (24); the output says so.

Every scratch container carries the label `bay.restore_test.expires`: `restore_keep_hours` for
a kept one, `restore_test_max_hours` (6) for a test, which removes its container at once when it
ends. The 6-hourly freshness run (`bay-backup-freshness`) removes an expired one with its own
volume (`docker rm -f -v`, only names that start with `bay-restore-test-`), so neither an
interrupted test nor a reboot leaves one behind. A kept container also gets a transient systemd
timer (`<name>-rm`) for the exact time; a reboot loses that timer, the label stays.

The scratch container takes the accessory's image, its compiled memory cap (`mem_limit`), its
`shm_size` and its `command` (so `shared_preload_libraries` and other `-c` settings load).
For a plain dump, the roles of the live server (one read-only query) are made `NOLOGIN` in the
scratch container first: a plain dump says `ALTER ... OWNER TO <role>`, and without the role
psql stops there. A custom dump restores with `--no-owner --no-privileges`.

The box must have the live `pg_database_size` plus a quarter (at least 1 GiB more) free on the
Docker data root, else the restore stops before it starts anything. When the live database does
not answer, the restore size of the snapshot from `restic stats`, twice, counts instead. No
pre-restore backup runs, because nothing live changes.

`--into live` restores into the running database. It always needs `--yes-stop-clients`, also
when no container would be stopped:

- The clients of the restored database that run on the restore host are stopped first and
  started again after, also when the restore fails. For a project database these are the other
  containers of the project; for a shared resource, the services bound to that database by a
  `database:` block (a service bound to another database of the same server keeps running).
  The command names them; the prompt names them again.
- After that, the client sessions still open on the database are listed (`pg_stat_activity`
  with `backend_type = 'client backend'`, without our own; autovacuum and extension workers do
  not count). Any left (a client on another box, a cron, a psql) stop the restore with their
  pid, application, client address and user; the clients start again and the lock goes away.
  `--terminate-connections` ends them with `pg_terminate_backend` instead.
- Only then the pre-restore backup runs (tag `pre-restore`): it holds every write up to the
  restore, and a refused attempt pays for no backup run.
- The restore runs with `PGOPTIONS=-c lock_timeout=30s` (`restore_lock_timeout`): a lock held by
  a session that slipped in fails the restore instead of a silent wait.
- While the clients are stopped, the restore holds `<backup_lock_dir>/restore-<target>.lock`.
  The nightly `docker system prune -af` skips its run (it removes stopped containers), a deploy
  stops before it changes a container, and a webhook rebuild refuses the recreate (exit row 28
  of the observability contract). A lock older than 12 hours is from a restore that died and is
  ignored. The lock goes away after the clients start, also on failure.
- The lock covers only a live pg_dump restore. A file, volume or Redis restore holds no lock.
  `bay provision` and `bay deploy --rig` do not check it either: the nftables handler restarts
  Docker, and that starts exited containers. Run none of these during a live restore.
- custom: `pg_restore --clean --if-exists --single-transaction --exit-on-error`. Each object
  of the dump is dropped before it is created, in one transaction; on an error nothing changes.
  It does not undo the rest: an object made after the snapshot (a table, a column of a later
  migration) stays, while a migrations table goes back to the snapshot, so the next migration
  can fail on an object that is already there. Check the schema after a live restore, or prove
  the snapshot in a scratch container first. The command says this before its prompt.
- plain: `psql` with `ON_ERROR_STOP` and `--single-transaction`. A plain `pg_dump` has no `DROP`
  statements, so restore into a database that does not hold the dumped objects. Over one that
  still has them, the restore stops at `already exists` and changes nothing.
- The result is checked (the database has tables).

Every snapshot holds one file and one database. `latest` takes the newest snapshot;
`--database <name>` takes only the snapshots of that database, and a `--snapshot` that holds
another database is refused. When the repo holds several databases and you name none, the
restore stops and names them: the newest snapshot may hold another database. One database
stored as `.sql` before a switch to the custom format and as `.dump` after is one database: the
newest snapshot wins.

Every restic call of a restore runs as root with `--no-cache`, so it never writes into the
cache of the backup unit.

Before 2.23.2 the dump never reached `psql` (`docker exec` without `-i`): the restore failed
with exit 141 or reported success, and restored nothing either way. Before 2.23.2
`bay backup restore` also started the playbook without the fleet's group_vars, so it stopped at
its first task.

### Restore test (Postgres)

`bay backup restore-test <env> <target>` runs the scratch restore with no prompt and removes
the container after, also on failure. It prints the tables with their exact row counts and the
live estimates, writes the report to `<backup dir>/status/<target>.restore-test.json` on the
box, and exits 0 when the restore worked and holds tables, else 1. `--json` prints one
document. Only counts leave the box. A failed test, and a failed `restore --into scratch`, sends
`backup.restore_test_failed` (warn): the live database was not touched, so it is not
`restore.failed`.

One test reads the whole snapshot from S3 once (S3 egress) and costs some minutes of box disk
and CPU. It is a manual command, never a timer, so it cannot repeat on its own.

The pre-restore backup can only be skipped with the playbook variable
`-e skip_pre_backup=true`; `bay backup restore` always takes it.

## Monitoring

- **Alerts** — backup failures, snapshot size warnings, and integrity check failures go to the alert recipients (see [alerting.md](alerting.md))
- **Freshness check** (since 2.24.0) — the timer `bay-backup-freshness.timer` runs every 6 hours on each box with backups. It reads `targets.json` (the targets the role installed), the status file each good run writes (`<backup dir>/status/<target>.json`) and the timer states. It sends `backup.missing` when a target has no script or no enabled, active timer, and `backup.stale` when a target had no good run for `max_age_hours` (default: 1.25 times the longest gap of the schedule, at least `backup_max_age_hours`, 30). One alert when the problem starts, then at most one per `backup_freshness_repeat_hours` (24) while it stays. It reads only local files, systemd and one `docker ps`: no restic and no S3, and it never starts a backup. The same run removes expired scratch containers (see PostgreSQL: scratch or live). With no status file yet, the clock starts at the later of the timer install and the manifest, so a new target, or a box just upgraded to 2.24.0, is not stale before it could run. A change of the target list rewrites the manifest and so restarts that clock.
- **`bay backup status`** — which targets each box should have, from the fleet config with the backup role's own rules, and what the box has: script, timer, last good run, next run. A target that was never installed shows as `missing`. Exit codes: `0` all fine, `1` a configured target is missing, `2` a target is stale, `3` a box did not answer (the lowest non-zero code wins). `--json` prints one document. `--deep` also lists the snapshots of every target (one S3 list each). A box whose role predates 2.24.0 writes no status file, so its targets show `no_record` until the next `bay up` (with `--deep`, the newest snapshot counts as the last good run). Before 2.24.0 the command parsed the coloured Ansible output: host lines became rows and every snapshot count read 0.
- **`bay backup list <target>`** — exits 1 when the target is in the config but no box has it installed.
- **`bay backup run [<target>]`** — starts `bay-backup@<target>.service` (every target of the env when you name none), the same unit as the timer: the app user, the alert credentials, the same status file. It waits for the run and prints its log. Before 2.24.0 it ran the script as root, and a root-owned restic cache made every later timer run go without a cache.
- **Journald** — all backup output goes to `journalctl -u bay-backup@<name>`
- **Systemd timers** — check schedules with `systemctl list-timers 'bay-backup@*'`

## Repository layout

Each accessory gets its own isolated restic repository:

```
s3:<endpoint>/<bucket>/<prefix>/<hostname>/<accessory-name>/
```

The default prefix is `backups`, so a typical path looks like `s3:s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/bay-ss/backups/web01/postgres/`. This keeps backup data separated from other objects in the same bucket.

This provides independent locking, independent retention, and failure isolation — a corrupted repo affects only one accessory.

## Defaults

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `backup_enabled` | `false` | Master switch — set to `true` in group_vars to enable |
| `backup_restic_version` | `0.17.3` | Restic binary version. The role installs it only when `backup_restic_bin` is missing, and stops when the binary there is older than 0.17.0 or is 0.20.0 or newer. Restic 0.19.x is accepted; the pin did not move |
| `backup_s3_endpoint` | `{{ secrets.backup_s3_endpoint \| default(S3_ENDPOINT) }}` | Set in `secrets:` dict; falls back to shared `S3_ENDPOINT` var |
| `backup_s3_bucket` | `{{ secrets.backup_s3_bucket \| default(S3_BUCKET) }}` | Set in `secrets:` dict; falls back to shared `S3_BUCKET` var |
| `backup_s3_access_key_id` | `{{ secrets.backup_s3_access_key_id \| default(S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID) }}` | Set in `secrets:` dict; falls back to shared `S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID` var |
| `backup_s3_secret_access_key` | `{{ secrets.backup_s3_secret_access_key \| default(S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY) }}` | Set in `secrets:` dict; falls back to shared `S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` var |
| `backup_s3_prefix` | `backups` | Prefix within the bucket (separates backup data from other objects) |
| `backup_schedule` | `0 3 * * *` | Default backup time (3 AM daily) |
| `backup_retain` | `30` | Default retention (30 days) |
| `backup_scripts_dir` | `/opt/<stack>/backup` | Backup scripts location |
| `backup_lock_dir` | `/opt/<stack>/backup/locks` | Lock files location |
| `backup_status_dir` | `/opt/<stack>/backup/status` | Status file of the last good run per target, alert state, restore test reports |
| `backup_max_age_hours` | `30` | The least hours without a good run before `backup.stale`; the default limit of a target is 1.25 times its longest schedule gap when that is more (per target: `max_age_hours`) |
| `restore_keep_hours` | `24` | Hours before a kept scratch container (`bay backup restore --into scratch`) expires |
| `restore_test_max_hours` | `6` | Hours before the scratch container of an interrupted restore test expires |
| `restore_lock_timeout` | `30s` | Postgres `lock_timeout` of a live restore |
| `backup_freshness_enabled` | `true` | Install the 6-hourly freshness check |
| `backup_freshness_schedule` | `*-*-* 00/6:17:00` | systemd `OnCalendar` of the freshness check |
| `backup_freshness_repeat_hours` | `24` | Hours between two alerts for the same problem |
| `backup_headscale_state` | `true` | Back up Headscale state on the control region (set `false` to disable) |
| `backup_headscale_container` | `headscale` | Container name backed up (also the restic repo/target name) |
| `backup_headscale_data_dir` | `/opt/headscale/data` | Host folder of the Headscale data (the DB snapshot and the noise/DERP keys come from here) |
| `backup_headscale_snapshot_bin` | `/usr/local/sbin/bay-headscale-db-snapshot` | Root helper that makes the checked DB snapshot |
| `backup_headscale_snapshot_dir` | `/var/lib/bay-headscale-backup` | Root-only (0700) folder for the temp snapshot |
| `backup_headscale_schedule` | `{{ backup_schedule }}` | Headscale backup schedule (defaults to the global schedule) |
| `backup_headscale_retain` | `{{ backup_retain }}` | Headscale retention (defaults to the global retention) |
